excerpt_i18n.en: Recently, a robotic duck only 25 centimeters tall unexpectedly thrust the imagination of edge AI into the spotlight. Microduck, released by Pollen Robotics under Hugging Face, is an open-source bipedal robot priced at $399. Weighing about 800 grams, it can walk, sit, kick a ball, and grasp objects out of the box, and it can even get back up on its own after falling. More importantly, it is not just a toy that moves—it is an open-source robotics platform for developers: users can train action policies in a simulated environment and then deploy them onto the real robot. This "little duck" has drawn attention not only because it is cute enough and cheap enough, nor simply because robots are finally making their way onto ordinary developers' desktops. The real signal it sends is this: AI is moving from models inside screens to physical devices that can perceive, act, and interact. Over the past few years, when people talked about AI, the conversation usually centered on cloud-based large models, parameter scale, training clusters, and compute centers. But when AI begins to enter the real world, the questions become very concrete: Can devices respond locally? Can they operate offline? Can private data stay off the cloud? Can power consumption and heat dissipation be acceptable to end devices? Can costs support large-scale adoption? These are exactly the questions that must be answered for edge AI to truly take root.
